reading.rtitle: The First Five, the Last Five
paras: Two HR meetings start at nine o'clock on the same Tuesday, in two different countries. Both have the same subject, the same number of participants and exactly one hour. One of them produces three decisions. The other one produces a second meeting.

In the first meeting, the person who opens says three things in ninety seconds: what is on the agenda, which point needs a decision and which one is only for information, and how much time each point has. Nobody has to guess what the hour is for.

In the middle, the discussion leaves the subject, as it always does. In the first meeting somebody says "going back to the point" and the group returns. In the second meeting the same thing happens and nobody says anything, because interrupting feels impolite. Twenty minutes later the real subject has four minutes left.

The difference appears again at the end. The first meeting stops five minutes before the hour. The chair says "to sum up", repeats the two decisions, reads the three action items with an owner and a date for each one, and names the point that is still open. In the second meeting the hour finishes, people leave, and everybody believes that somebody else is going to send an email.

The minutes arrive the same afternoon in one case and never in the other. Nothing here is about language level or about seniority. It is about five sentences at the start and five sentences at the end, and about one person deciding to say them.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- text written for this lesson; the two meetings are illustrative and no real meeting is described

gist.prompt: What makes the difference between the two meetings?
choices: The first meeting had more time and fewer participants.
In the first meeting, somebody opened, brought the discussion back and closed with owners and dates.
The people in the second meeting were less senior and less prepared.

items: In the first meeting, the opening says which point needs a decision.
'which point needs a decision and which one is only for information'
The discussion only left the subject in the second meeting.
'the discussion leaves the subject, as it always does' -- it happens in both.
In the second meeting, nobody brought the discussion back because interrupting felt impolite.
'nobody says anything, because interrupting feels impolite'
The first meeting used the full hour and closed exactly on time.
'The first meeting stops five minutes before the hour.'
According to the text, the difference comes from the level of English of the participants.
'Nothing here is about language level or about seniority.'

items.situation: Everybody is in the room and it is nine o'clock.
tips: Let's get started. We have three points today.
Do not wait for somebody else to open.

items.situation: Somebody is speaking and you have one important detail.
tips: If I may add, the effective date is a holiday in Chile.
One short signal, then your point.

items.situation: The discussion has left the agenda for five minutes.
tips: Going back to the point, we still need a decision on the two positions.
Name the point you are returning to.

items.situation: The first point is finished and nobody is moving.
tips: If there are no questions, let us move on to the next point.
move ON TO the next point.
We have five minutes left, so let us wrap up.
Close before the hour, not after it.

items.situation: You are closing and you want to name the action.
tips: The next step is a proposal from finance by Friday.
Every close ends with a person and a date.

listenings.text: Good morning everyone, and thank you for being on time. Let's get started. We have three points today and one hour. The first point is the headcount of the month: that one is for information, and it takes ten minutes. The second point is the remote work policy, also for information, because the decision was taken at headquarters last week. The third point is the open positions in Chile, and that one is for decision, so I want to leave at least twenty minutes for it. Two things before we start. Please keep each point to ten minutes, and if you have a document, send it before the meeting and not during it. Right, let me kick off with the headcount numbers.

We have five minutes left, so let us wrap up. To sum up, we took two decisions today. First, one position in Chile is approved and can be published this week. Second, the other position stays on hold until finance confirms the budget for the quarter. Then we have three action items. HR sends the local adaptation to headquarters by the tenth. Finance confirms the budget by Friday. And the country manager speaks to his team this week, before anybody reads the policy somewhere else. One point stays open: the effective date falls on a Sunday and we still have to check that. I write the minutes and send them to all of you before the end of the afternoon. Thank you, everyone.
